author: rbren

body:
Re: inheritance, I added some more notes to the docstring on Plan.

Ultimately, we have a tree structure representing the agent's plan, e.g.

* Do x
  * Do x'
  * Do x''
    * Do x''1
    * Do x''2
* Do y
  * Do y'
    * Do y''
* Do z


What's odd about this data structure is that the top-level is a list, not a single node. So to hold onto it, we need a sort of invisible root node. That's where `Plan` comes in.

`Plan` needs to be the same type as every other node, so that `parent` references work nicely. But it's also a special node that doesn't contain any information itself, hence the subclassing.

I'm open to other suggestions here, but this is the best I've come up with
author: rbren

body: Thanks @rbren , I'm still a bit confused though. Why couldn't we just use `Task` for the top-level node too?
author: neubig

body: We need to e.g. override the `__init__` so that it doesn't try and set an `id` etc
author: rbren

body:
What about something like this?

```python
class Task:
    def __init__(
        self,
        parent: 'Task' | None,
        goal: str,
        state: str = OPEN_STATE,
        subtasks: list = [],
    ):
        """Initializes a new instance of the Task class.

        Args:
            parent: The parent task, or None if it is the root task.
            goal: The goal of the task.
            state: The initial state of the task.
            subtasks: A list of subtasks associated with this task.
        """
        if parent is None:
            self.id = ''
        elif parent.id:
            self.id = parent.id + '.' + str(len(parent.subtasks))
        else:
            self.id = str(len(parent.subtasks))
        self.parent = parent
        self.goal = goal
        self.subtasks = []
        for subtask in subtasks or []:
            if isinstance(subtask, Task):
                self.subtasks.append(subtask)
            else:
                goal = subtask.get('goal')
                state = subtask.get('state')
                subtasks = subtask.get('subtasks')
                self.subtasks.append(Task(self, goal, state, subtasks))

        self.state = OPEN_STATE
```

then for `Plan` we call `Task(None, '', OPEN_STATE, subtasks)`?

Note that the only thing I changed is the first `if parent is None` part.
author: neubig

body:
That works!

The bigger issue I think are the helper methods that are defined on Plan: `get_task_by_id`, `add_subtask`, and `set_subtask_state`. Calling these on a non-root Task would cause problems.

Two things I could do:
* Make these normal functions, instead of class methods, which take in a task param
* Put an `assert` at the top of the function making sure the task it's called on is a root task

The downside is we lose type safety--the code can call those functions on a non-root task, and we'd just get a runtime error. 

WDYT?
author: rbren

body:
Thanks @rbren , I think the "assert" thing should probably be fine for now?

And I feel that (eventually, not in this PR) we might even be able to just set this up so there's not really any distinction between a top-level plan and a task at all. After all, tasks themselves can also have subtasks. I don't think there's anything really all that special about the one at the top of the hierarchy versus the ones in the middle of the hierarchy.

edit: I think this is what you are already doing, but the terminology `Plan` makes it seem completely different than a `Task`, when it is just a more abstract version of the same idea.

I'm unsure if this will affect the integration tests.Here is the files for both [successful](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/files/15306075/successful.md) and [failed](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/files/15306076/failed.md) tests.

I don't yet have a clue, maybe due to some sandbox issues? How do you run local integration tests? by running the `TEST_ONLY=true ./tests/integration/regenerate.sh`?
author: xingyaoww

body:
> by running the `TEST_ONLY=true ./tests/integration/regenerate.sh`?

Yes. And to make it easier to write/run the new integration test, I set the environment variables `TARGET_AGENT` and `TARGET_TEST`.

```
TARGET_AGENT="CodeActAgent" TARGET_TEST="test_ipython_installation" ./tests/integration/regenerate.sh
``` 
 
The issues with failed integration tests, both locally and in GitHub Actions, are due to two main causes: the statefulness of the sandbox environment and the prompt containing an excessively long installation log.

To resolve these issues, I propose two solutions:

1. Ignore the cache to ensure that the tests are consistent on every run.
2. Ignore the installation log that is too long, which may cause the LLM completion to fail.
```
pip install --no-cache-dir pandas > /dev/null 2>&1
```

I have already resolved these issues in my forked OpenDevin.

I'm wondering what the other maintainers think about PR templates -- I think some structure is good, but too much structure adds extra red tape that takes time.

Personally I think that something like this but a little simpler might be good. For instance:

```markdown
<!-- please describe the PR so that others reviewing understand the motivation -->

<!-- if this fixes an issue, please write "Fixes [issue_url]" so the issue is auto-closed -->

<!-- please check if you added unit tests for new code, and add them if not -->
```

We may revisit this decision later, but we'll close this PR for now. We'd definitely welcome other contributions though!

> 
>

Gotcha, I wasn't aware before. @JensRoland do you only get "Error creating controller: Could not establish connection to host" with :? If not, we can revert.
author: yimothysu

body:
@yimothysu correct, I got the error when using `:` but not using `=` (on MacOS Sonoma on an M1 Mac running Colima 0.6.8 and Docker 26.1.2)

If you look closely at that Docker documentation page, it shows two valid syntaxes:

```sh
$ docker run --add-host my-hostname=8.8.8.8
$ docker run --add-host=my-hostname:8.8.8.8
```

If I'm understanding that correctly, the `:` is used in combination with an `=` character separating the `--add-host` and the host value. The way it was written in the README was this:

```sh
$ docker run --add-host my-hostname:8.8.8.8
```

which as far as I can tell is not an explicitly supported syntax.

body: @rbren The major issue of that is, when controller sets agent to other states, it completely reset the state for a new task (all histories are removed). We need to store the state before it got reseted, or we need to mess around with the set agent state which could be more complex.

body:
Sounds like y'all are on it, but just want to agree--if there's an issue with the LLM response, we should raise an `Agent*` error, so that the message gets passed back to the LLM on the next turn instead of breaking the loop.

(Also we should rename `LLMOutputError` to something like `AgentLLMOutputError` so that we can be consistent here)
author: rbren

body:
@enyst Thank you so much for your detailed and constructive feedback on the PR!

>If the LLM sends something that we cannot adapt to (e.g. 'kill pid'), then:
prefer to send back the error to the LLM, so that next time it does better, hopefully
if that's not possible, fail, set state to ERROR or whatever we need to do


I prefer this approach. Perhaps we can convert `Pydantic's ValidationError` into a custom `Agent*Error`. However, I'm not entirely sure about the best way to proceed with this task. I welcome any help and encourage others to contribute to this PR. Perhaps we should close this PR for now until we find the right solution? @li-boxuan

Agree. I appreciate your efforts and in hindsight, I didn't think of this problem thoroughly when I opened the issue. If you'd like to, I guess we could add a comment to the test, explaining that the "errors" are actually "features" rather than "bugs", but up to you.

body: I believe the release is meaningful because: Releases can accommodate more content, allowing for a clear display of different versions, showcasing the features and fixes made in each version, and attributing the work to specific contributors (which can increase their sense of achievement). body:
@li-boxuan Re: your question about 3 times: good question! My thinking is like this: we have a set of events, they're too large, and the last few matter. Constraint: the summarize prompt might (and does, in practice!) run into ContextWindowExceeded itself, if it's sent with all recent events.

The PR is attempting two naive approaches to make it work better:
- condense half, repeat if still necessary. I tested with 5 times, and reduced it. If the need for condense happened when there were 30 events (which can happen, though not with GPT-4-1106 or the like), then 3 is almost too many times, because in the worse case (each half resulted in 1-2 summary events; but it still needs), we're left with very few fully detailed.
- just tell the LLM to prioritize later events. I'm not sure if that works well with the PR prompt. 😢 I think it stopped being worse than the current prompt. IMHO it has the potential to work _better_ than some naive in-code approach, and I've considered to drop the first and just keep and iterate on this one.
 
Still, I think we need _something_ to deal with the possibility that summarizing all events in the same time errors out. Even if it's only 1 round with a subset. This PR doesn't attempt to make a good summarization, just make it work more times than it does. (and take some more stuff out of monologue)

I don't know, perhaps @rbren or @xingyaoww can tell if this PR makes it better or worse, or should we just cut monologue out until the condensing process is ready for CodeAct and then we see, or some other alternative.

Side note:
What this PR also doesn't do, since it doesn't touch the last events, is deal with a funny case: the last observation was significantly larger than the rest. Like when GPT-4 escaped on the internet and came back with more than 80k tokens - good times! It doesn't deal with it because that case should be handled now, we have elsewhere code that trims the output to a low number of characters (hard-coded 5000 for monologue I believe); and we have also code that removes "heavy stuff" like screenshots that weren't supposed to be sent anyway. That should work. Give or take that I've seen some weird things, that I can't replicate, like output from docker spilling over... somehow. Perhaps it was before all these other measures were put in place.

body:
@rbren right now, one session-id maps to one EventStream instance? And events are stored under the sid dir.  But the delegated agent(like CoderAgent) shares event-stream with DelegateAgent, 
```
 async def start_delegate(self, action: AgentDelegateAction):
        AgentCls: Type[Agent] = Agent.get_cls(action.agent)
        agent = AgentCls(llm=self.agent.llm)
        self.delegate = AgentController(
            sid=self.id + '-delegate',
            agent=agent,
            event_stream=self.event_stream,
            max_iterations=self.max_iterations,
            max_chars=self.max_chars,
            inputs=action.inputs,
        )
```
when initializing AgentController, 
```
 self.event_stream.subscribe(
            EventStreamSubscriber.AGENT_CONTROLLER, self.on_event
        )
```
the `AGENT_CONTROLLER` will be subscribed twice and exception will be thrown due to this change:
```
 def subscribe(self, id: EventStreamSubscriber, callback: Callable):
        if id in self._subscribers:
            logger.warning('Subscriber subscribed multiple times: ' + id)
->        raise ValueError('Subscriber already exists: ' + id)
```

So, what's your opinion on the event management of agents created by the main agent?

body:
@amanape the big motivation is that we need to stop going directly to the local filesystem for `list-files`, and instead start leaning on the `runtime`. E.g. if we're using an E2B runtime, we need to list files _there_, not in the local directory.

It's generally easier (and more efficient) to support a non-recursive list, so I found myself making this change as part of https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/1810, but that PR started getting a little out of hand so I factored it out.

> I didn't understand why a web server can help in this case. Do you mean moving file into the web server and let gymnasium can access the file url just like browsing the web?

Since the browser already have screenshot support in our codebase, as well as support for more complex file handling (e.g. the browser can open PDF files, but not so much for the cmdline), by allowing the browser to access files inside the sandbox's workspace should enable such scenario. Also, if the multimodal LLM takes in browser screenshot images in the future, this could be a way of unifying visual observation of various files. Still, we could still do filetype-specific handling as the other PR you mentioned is doing. 

As for the web server thing - original I thought the files in the sandbox will not be directly accessible to the browser running on host. But after checking, it seems like /workspace is mounted from host, so that maybe the browser can directly open these files with file://

author: li-boxuan

body:
@li-boxuan Thanks for your comment! I agree with your insight that the entity deduction doesn't directly contribute to the code. After talking with @xingyaoww, we see two potential benefits of adding benchmarks that don't strictly focus on coding issues. These benchmarks with clear evaluation could possibly demonstrate the general ability to solve multi-turn tasks involving planning, helping us assess whether coding-based pre-training/fine-tuning could extrapolate to other domains that require similar planning and reasoning skills.

On the other side, it might be worth testing whether the model has the capability to ask questions to find needle in the haystack. Currently, our agent relies on the user to initiate and steer the conversation. However, in situations where the user lacks experience, they may depend on the agent to take the lead in the interaction. In such cases, the agent may need to transition to an approach where it initiates the conversation based on understanding the user's intent and proactively provides information. Of course, this is a stretching goal, but it might be helpful to start building some proxy evaluation tasks to test on this.

body:
@li-boxuan 

> I am a little bit confused about how this PR addresses [#1910 (comment)](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/1910#discussion_r1606940945). Do you mind elaborating?

If we introduce rules like B006 and B008 pre-commit, then we address issues like this:

https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/1713

before they happen. I really think we should do this, even if take in only these two rules.

I can see why the relationship with that comment is not clear, wow, my bad. Fixing the reference now.

What I mean is: the issues caused by mutable defaults can be annoying or serious enough to lead to over correction in other parts of the code. I think 1713 tilted the balance towards needing to raise an exception [here](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/1910/files/9c719cf25a3b4fb2004c0091023d5b0126e88526#diff-081383e511233feb06a2eaef61d764a8543aa7b8229e1352ac05eacc74400233L67).

To be clear, I'm just guessing, I don't think Robert said that explicitly. It's just my opinion about why the code is shaping up in a particular way, and it's why I didn't comment on it.

Allow me to take another example: the custom `llm_config` feature you suggested has proven amazingly useful in ways I didn't realize at the time, and I'm so glad you brought it out! During its implementation, I frankly thought it was going to be easy, and it ended up taking far more time than I had possibly guessed. Why? It's a bit embarrassing to admit, I wasted hours because of this python behavior.

The reason there was that unlike other config-related things, this one has to happen after everything was set up, and after a bunch of other imports happen. Those imports initialize damn parameters... with values that never change when you execute the call.

`llmconfig` was updated before _execution_ of function calls, with a custom group of settings, but function calls were never receiving the update. And I didn't see it. I suspected everything else on the execution path, reasonable or otherwise, except this Python behavior...

This behavior is as old as Python. Now this Ruff automation won't solve every kind of parameter passing in those issues I've had, but it will solve some. And it will attract our attention, reminding us it's happening. I believe we should automate it, instead of working around or wasting more time anywhere else.

> I have not read the original paper. Could you tell me the difference between `original ProntoQA` and this implementation?

From my understanding, the original implementation gives the model the rules, and facts via natural language context, and from the query the model has to derive the series of proof steps to come up with the answer for the query. Regarding this implementation, I think the author is trying to convert the context and query to code for the agent to execute and obtain the final result.

> Do you have any other idea?

I'm not sure, but thinking about not feeding the raw program to the agent and instead letting it formulate the program by itself.
author: ryanhoangt

body:
> > I have not read the original paper. Could you tell me the difference between `original ProntoQA` and this implementation?
> 
> From my understanding, the original implementation gives the model the rules, and facts via natural language context, and from the query the model has to derive the series of proof steps to come up with the answer for the query. Regarding this implementation, I think the author is trying to convert the context and query to code for the agent to execute and obtain the final result.
> 
> > Do you have any other idea?
> 
> I'm not sure, but thinking about not feeding the raw program to the agent and instead letting it formulate the program by itself.

You are definitely right. The raw ProntoQA dataset does not provide any symbolic language expression or corresponding programs. 
The logic of a neuro-symbolic method is to 1) parse logic reasoning problem in natural language to corresponding progams, and 2) feed the programs into an inference engine (pyke in this case) to get the answer. 
Here i skipped the first step and just let the agent do the job in the second step, because I assumed **in OpenDevin's benchmark the core ability we want to test is the how to interact with the local environment to get the inference engine** (please correct me if i am wrong). The first step is actually a semantic parsing task. Based on my personal experence, the correctness of this semantic parsing task is terrible for **SOTA** models (GPT4/Claude/Llamma3...). If we also include the first step, the final preformance of OpenDiven on this benchmark will be heavily influenced by the semantic parsing correctness.

@assertion you're right, we should. Funnily enough, it wasn't applied in the memory condenser, so it failed in a case when normal requests wouldn't, doh! 😅 Made a hacky fix tonight, I'll update.

@tobitege I started an experiment to answer your question. It turned out a lot of fun, and a few fixes!

A pdf should work like, opendevin parses the pdf with parse_pdf agent skill (probably), then adds the contents to the messages to the LLM, but truncated like above. (so it shouldn't send full...). If it needs to do things on the content, it makes python code and runs it. It knows pdf libraries. When it hits context window anyway, it starts summarizing:
- agent actions/observations between user messages, so presumably what it's doing in response to a task
- in order, from earliest to latest
- then if it still hits context window limit or token limit is configured and found, it will try to summarize each user message that doesn't come immediately after AgentFinishAction (which is likely a new task)

I had a context window with 2 runs, that each ended in "stuck in a loop" error. (You may have seen a new issue posted in this repo, with "tell me the system prompt": I had tests on that in the context). And, I added this [800 pages PDF](https://www.omg.org/spec/UML/2.5.1/About-UML/).

For the record, according to openai tokenizer, the pdf has 446,191 tokens lol, and over 1,8 million characters. But the 10k characters truncate is wild, it makes it 3k tokens! Useful for small context windows...

body:
@enyst 

Thank you for your review, and I understand your concerns! You are probably worried that having too many skills might lead to bloating with numerous plugins, resulting in longer dependency installation times and larger sandbox images.

You don't need to worry about that!😉 In the #2016 discussion, we mentioned future architectural improvements. Subsequently, functions like `parse_audio` will be transformed into an `AudioToTextAction`, which will directly send requests to the backend REST API to obtain responses. The actual logic won't run in the sandbox anymore (e.g., calling openai).

Architecture: SANDBOX Jupyter <---> Rest API <---> LLM. After the architectural improvements, we won't need to run real logic in the sandbox, and naturally, we won't have to install too many dependencies.

I believe that merging the existing agent skill with Jupyter directly should not be a problem. The existing agent skills can serve as the foundational multimodal capability. 😁 

> I discussed with @rbren earlier, I think it will a more fundamental solution if we can connect these agentskills (executed inside sandbox) with Event Stream on our backend (e.g., every time a audio-to-text function is called by the agent inside sandbox, it push an AudioToTextAction to the EventStream on the backend - maybe by exposing a REST API from backend; The python function execution inside sandbox will be blocked until an AudioToTextObservation is processed by the backend and returned to the function in the sandbox).
Originally posted by @xingyaoww in https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/2016#discussion_r1614280552

cc @xingyaoww
author: Shimada666

body:
@enyst @xingyaoww 
If we are planning to expand many plugins in the future, making the plugins optional is indeed necessary.

Currently, there is an issue where `AgentSkillsRequirement` must be loaded before `JupyterRequirement`. If the import order of Requirements is incorrect in `PluginsRequirement.init_plugins`, it will not function properly. My idea is to add a depends_on option in PluginRequirement, for example, `AgentSkillsRequirement` depends_on [`JupyterRequirement`]. Simultaneously, rewriting the logic in `init_plugins` to automatically load based on priority will eliminate the need for enforcing import order.

At the same time, in our sandbox Dockerfile, we only install basic dependencies (such as `Jupyter`). Additional dependencies are still installed in the `setup.sh` of the plugins. If needed in the future, we can consider customizing a sandbox docker image for each agent, containing all the dependencies required by the agent.

body:
### Description:

This pull request is to introduce an evaluation on the BioCoder dataset using agents on OpenDevin. The Biocoder benchmark aims to assess the performance of LLMs on entire repositories related to bioinformatics. It is a challenging full-repository level benchmark that requires both understanding of long-range, inter-class dependencies and domain knowledge.

By evaluating this dataset, we can gain further insights on the performance of LLMs on closed domain (bioinformatics) tasks, as well as their ability to retrieve information and relevant code from a large context window, or the entire repository.

### Key changes:
Added `evaluation/biocoder/run_infer.py`: This file handles execution of the entire Biocoder benchmark using OpenDevin. It loads datasets, runs the agent on each task, and saves the evaluation outputs. Note that we are still 
Added `evaluation/biocoder/biocoder_env_box.py`: This file handles setting up the Biocoder docker environment (which contains many dependencies, libraries, and environments shared across the repositories in Biocoder, including downloading repository files and metadata.

Updated `README.md`: We have updated the README.md to include information about Biocoder, such as the design, challenges, and objectives of the benchmark. Furthermore, we include documentations on executing the framework, an example of the evaluation, and instructions for contributing and customization.

### Related papers:
BioCoder: A Benchmark for Bioinformatics Code Generation with Large Language Models (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.16458)

body:
Interesting discussion and I totally agree with @SmartManoj that the default reply needs changing.

However, the `create_file` method's non-standard behavior is giving me headaches by raising an exception if the file already exists. And I don't see external tools like "touch" as the standard as it has a different purpose.

In most languages I know the code would overwrite the existing file, unless there are permission issues, even Python.

I'd expect the same behavior here. If the actual file `open` command in `create_file` raises an exception, that is expected and the LLM should understand the error message just as fine.

Otherwise, the LLM should return a factual message like `[File xxx opened in writing mode.]` as that is what it expects, and not just `[File xxx (0 lines total)]` and leave it guessing, as was pointed out earlier.

In general, if OD *can* provide helpful replies, it should do it and not rely on the LLM interpreting ambiguous messages.

Just wanted to quickly put in one vote for @tobitege 's proposal making our agent skills as similar as possible to the standard behavior of existing functions in Python. Like us, models "know" (to some extent) the standard behavior of operating systems, and so having the behavior be expected rather than unexpected seems like a good idea.

In this case I think that would be either:
* Overwrite (like `echo "file" > existing_file.txt`)
* Do not create, and throw failure message (like `mkdir existing_file.txt`)

body:
Since the plugins depend on sshd for execution, we must include sshd in the image. In the previous example, I installed sshd in Ubuntu by specifying the entrypoint, and it successfully ran on Ubuntu 18.04/Debian 12, like this:
```python3
            self.container = self.docker_client.containers.run(
                self.container_image,
                entrypoint='bash',
                # allow root login
                user='root',
                command=f"-c \"apt update && apt install openssh-server;mkdir /var/run/sshd && mkdir -p -m0755 /var/run/sshd;/usr/sbin/sshd -D -p {self._ssh_port} -o 'PermitRootLogin=yes'\"",
                **network_kwargs,
                working_dir=self.sandbox_workspace_dir,
                name=self.container_name,
                detach=True,
                volumes=self.volumes,
            )
```
However, this approach is undoubtedly ugly and not universal. For instance, it doesn't apply to CentOS (which uses yum). Therefore, this PR does not include that part. Currently, it still requires an image with sshd built in to run, like `ghcr.io/opendevin/sandbox:main`.

After discussing with @xingyaoww, maybe we should abandon SSH and switch to using WebSocket communication. in future refactoring. A better approach is for users to provide a base image (CentOS/Ubuntu/Debian), from which we generate a Dockerfile to install the necessary runtime, rebuild the sandbox image, and then use this image.

So, I plan for this PR to be used only for isolating the Python environment for opendevin and creating image caches to speed up startup times. When use_cache is set to true in config.toml, the sandbox cache image will be automatically generated after the first run, and this cache image will be used in subsequent runs to reduce the startup time of the sandbox. You can test it with the following command

config.toml
```toml
[core]
...
use_cache = false
sandbox_container_image = "ghcr.io/opendevin/sandbox:main"
```

run command
```python
python3 opendevin/runtime/docker/ssh_box.py
```

Currently, I am using the Python base environment (3.10) provided by miniforge as the runtime for opendevin. If needed, it is also easy to install Python 3.11 and use it as the runtime, with the trade-off being a slightly slower startup time the first time it is launched.

body:
@li-boxuan @xingyaoww @yufansong 
Thank you very much for your help! I found the root cause of the issue: under the root user, pip points to `/opendevin/miniforge3/bin/pip` (because `/opendevin/miniforge3/bin` was added to the PATH in the Dockerfile), while under the opendevin user, pip points to `/usr/bin/pip`. This causes the opendevin user to use the system environment's pip when installing packages, which is why it doesn't work as expected.

```Dockerfile
# ==== OpenDevin Runtime Client ====
RUN mkdir -p /opendevin && mkdir -p /opendevin/logs && chmod 777 /opendevin/logs
RUN wget "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
RUN bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh -b -p /opendevin/miniforge3
RUN bash -c ". /opendevin/miniforge3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && conda config --set changeps1 False && conda config --append channels conda-forge"

# this
RUN echo "export PATH=/opendevin/miniforge3/bin:$PATH" >> ~/.bashrc
```

To solve this problem, I found a feasible solution: write the common configuration, such as PATH, into the global bashrc file. Modify the Dockerfile to change `echo "export PATH=/opendevin/miniforge3/bin:$PATH" >> ~/.bashrc` to `echo "export PATH=/opendevin/miniforge3/bin:$PATH" >> /etc/bash.bashrc`, and then before each plugin loads, run `source /etc/bash.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc`. This way, every user can recognize the correct pip path.

It has an additional benefit: it automatically points `python` to `/opendevin/miniforge3/bin/python` without any special setup. This way, using python in `setup.sh` will utilize `/opendevin/miniforge3/bin/python`.

```python
class PluginMixin:
    """Mixin for Sandbox to support plugins."""

    def _source_bashrc(self):
        exit_code, output = self.execute('source /etc/bash.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc')
        if exit_code != 0:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f'Failed to source ~/.bashrc with exit code {exit_code} and output: {output}'
            )
        logger.info('Sourced ~/.bashrc successfully')

    def init_plugins(self: SandboxProtocol, requirements: list[PluginRequirement]):
        """Load a plugin into the sandbox."""

        if hasattr(self, 'plugin_initialized') and self.plugin_initialized:
            return

        if self.initialize_plugins:
            logger.info('Initializing plugins in the sandbox')

            # clean-up ~/.bashrc and touch ~/.bashrc
            exit_code, output = self.execute('rm -f ~/.bashrc && touch ~/.bashrc')

            for requirement in requirements:
                self._source_bashrc()
            ...
```



Do you have any good suggestions?

body:
As @xingyaoww mentioned, I agree with placing enviroment in `/opendevin/bash.bashrc`.

I believe one of our design principles is to minimize the intrusiveness of opendevin, avoiding disruption to the system's original environment and instead isolating a separate environment for opendevin's use. Therefore, using `/opendevin/bash.bashrc` instead of `/etc/bash.bashrc` is preferable.

Based on this principle, we can place common environment variables in `/opendevin/bash.bashrc` rather than intruding into the user's original bashrc file. At the same time, we won't modify the system's original user's Python; instead, we will specify the Python to be used by sourcing the environment variables in the code when needed. This approach ensures that when users call Python, it still points to the system's original Python (`/usr/bin/python`). In summary, we can make opendevin a pluggable software, ensuring that it does not adversely affect the original environment.

I plan to create a PR to add environment variables to `/opendevin/bash.bashrc` in the Dockerfile. After the new PR is merged, I will modify this PR to load the environment variables from `/opendevin/bash.bashrc`, thereby accommodating both the root and opendevin users. Finally, I will remove the PATH in `/root/.bashrc` to ensure it does not affect the original container environment.

Isn't it possible that the .bashrc contains a (yet unidentified) command that could cause a user interaction and "cause" the hanging still, regardless of where the "source" is called?
I'm not a Linux guy, so had to ask my buddy WizardLM2 and got this as a reply, if that makes sense:
```
def start_ssh_session(self):
    self.__ssh_login()

    # Instead of sourcing .bashrc directly, you can selectively execute non-interactive parts of it.
    # This is a workaround to prevent hanging due to interactive commands in .bashrc.
    try:
        self.ssh.sendline("source /etc/profile.d/*.sh")  # Source system-wide profiles
        self.ssh.prompt()
        self.ssh.sendline("if [ -z \"$PS1\" ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi")  # Condition to avoid interactive parts
        self.ssh.prompt()
    except pxssh.ExceptionPxssh as e:
        logger.exception('Failed to source .bashrc: %s', e)
        raise e

    # Fix: https://github.com/pexpect/pexpect/issues/669
    self.ssh.sendline("bind 'set enable-bracketed-paste off'")
    self.ssh.prompt()
    # cd to workspace
    self.ssh.sendline(f'cd {self.sandbox_workspace_dir}')
    self.ssh.prompt()
```
Further annotation was:
"This modification attempts to source only the parts of .bashrc that are safe for non-interactive sessions. It checks for the presence of the PS1 variable, which is typically set in interactive shells, to decide whether to source .bashrc."

body: A counter-argument: agent skills should only accept skills that are non-trivial to implement. Appending could be easily done via python or bash commands, and we probably shouldn't prompt LLM to use it.
author: li-boxuan

body:
> A counter-argument: agent skills should only accept skills that are non-trivial to implement. Appending could be easily done via python or bash commands, and we probably shouldn't prompt LLM to use it.

There are several logistical, technical and economic advantages of an explicit `append_file` command:
- An "append" is easier to understand and does not require the LLM to first determine the last line number of a file.
- We cannot require or presume, that the targeted file has a trailing blank line (unlike linted Python source files) that could easily be "replaced". But even that blank line might be intended and needed to be preserved.
- The LLM may then intransparently decide to replace that last content line ("empty" or not) **or** wrongly come up with a line number higher than the current line count (as in above screenshot).
- It may itself need to create an extra Python script to determine the correct line number, requiring extra turns, raising time and cost. And that potentially for any subsequent part of a repetitive task (e.g. iterate files in folders for summarizations).

Above is "trivial" for us, but with the current implementation it is not a cost-effective and seemingly "harder" way for the LLM to achieve results.

**Major question:**
Alternatively, could `edit_file's` behavior be slightly changed, that IF the LLM's `start` line number is higher then the actual file's line count do an append automatically?  
Is the behavior more determined due to CodeActAgent needing Python file generation being strict?

**Potential PR changes**
When I started this PR, I intentionally stayed away from changing the core `edit_file`, just to be safe.
However, I could easily imagine the edit_file and potential append_file methods use a protected common method with "append" just being a boolean parameter, which certainly would reduce the agentskills codebase.

body:
Hi @neubig, can you please have a look and give some reviews if this implementation is aligned with what you're thinking of?

Some questions:
- Currently, I assume the workspace is a git repo and the repo map is built only from the tracked files (this is also what the authors do for `aider`). But I'm not sure what to do with the workspace that isn't a git repo. If we consider all files there will be cache dir, `node_modules`, etc
- When the workspace is large e.g. with OpenDevin code base, the construction of repomap seems to delay the ux quite a bit and also increase the cost. Not sure if we can improve this somehow?
- When `aider` builds a repo map, it excludes the files that are added to the chat (since the files' content is already there). But in OpenDevin we don't have files added to chat, so maybe we can simply consider all files?

body:
@ryanhoangt  Ughh, maybe it is not a good idea for me to directly push to your branch (maybe make things more messy) - feel free to revert if you want!

So I:
- make `ENABLE_REPOMAP` a configurable thing in the config
- and add `repomap_workspace`, which will default to `workspace_base` as you described earlier
- did some tweak in the SWE-Bench `run_infer.py` to set `repomap_workspace` to the corresponding github repo directory (e.g., `/workspace/XXX`) instead of `/workspace`.

You can run it by set your `config.toml`:

```
[core]
cache_dir = "/tmp/swe_bench_eval_cache_root"
workspace_base = "/home/xingyaow/OpenDevin-dev/workspace"
workspace_mount_path = "/home/xingyaow/OpenDevin-dev/workspace"
sandbox_container_image = "ghcr.io/opendevin/sandbox:main"
sandbox_type = "ssh"
ssh_hostname = "localhost"
sandbox_timeout = 120
max_chars = 100_000_000

# SWEBench eval specific
use_host_network = false
run_as_devin = false
enable_auto_lint = true
persist_sandbox = false
enable_repomap = true

[eval_gpt4o_2024_05_13]
temperature = 0.0
model = "gpt-4o-2024-05-13"
api_key = "sk-proj-YOURKEY"
```

AND RUN `evaluation/swe_bench/scripts/run_infer.sh eval_gpt4o_2024_05_13 HEAD CodeActAgent 1` to reproduce.

However, there are some issues with file permissions.
- By default, SWE-Bench does not mount the host workspace into the docker container since it already has everything (e.g., testbed, environment) built into it. However, the current implementation of `RepoMap` requires the **backend** to access the workspace directory. This makes supporting the current SWE-Bench eval very challenging.
- To overcome this, I added a workaround (https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/2248/commits/7e718d77855841056d0ffc741336c785b87f0dba) to support mounting the host directory into containers - But since inside the container, the agent is working on SWE-Bench problem as "root," so it will create the `/workspace/reponame_repoversion` folder with the root user.
- And on the host machine, the `RepoMap` code will try to create files under `/workspace/reponame_repoversion` - which will cause permission issue: You cannot create something under a directory owned by root.

I'm still thinking about a workaround, but I guess long-term it will be nice if we can put this RepoMap utility into `od-runtime-cli` proposed in https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/issues/2404 so that the RepoMap can be constructed within the runtime and passed back to the backend -- This will save us from wrestling with file permissions. cc @yufansong .

body:
>  we'll need to adjust the prompt to make the agent call the function when needed right?

Yes - or we can simulate the execution by calling that `agentskills` *for* the agent in a certain way (e.g., issuing an `IPythonRunCellAction` for every turn and get a repo map to put into user message) - it will be much clearer how we can do this once we finish the arch refractor https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/issues/2404

> So with your current integration, can we run some instances to quickly evaluate the effectiveness of injecting RepoMap in every step? (which is different when we move it to agentskills I think)

Not really.. So the issue is that the agent is running as `root` inside the container, and the current RepoMap implementation operates on the mounted workspace (`/workspace`) where the agent creates/edits files as `root.`
In https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/2490, I added some hacks to make all the files in `/workspace` be owned by a group that contains both `root` and the host user -- so that the host user can also read and create files there.
However, Once an agent touches a file, it may change the ownership of that file back to `root` again, causing the backend on the host to have permission errors in reading that file. So, the repo map may not be correctly generated AFTER the first step.

body:
Open PRs (Pull Requests) should not be closed when they lack changes because:

 - **Preservation of Ideas:** Keeping the PR open allows the original idea to be preserved. Future contributors can pick up where the original author left off, preventing the need to start from scratch.

 - **Encouragement for Collaboration:** An open PR signals to other developers that collaboration and further improvements are welcome. This can lead to community-driven development and enhancement of the original concept.

 - **Historical Context:** Open PRs provide historical context for why certain changes were proposed. This can be valuable for understanding the evolution of a project and the rationale behind certain decisions.

 - **Avoiding Duplication of Effort:** By marking a PR as a draft, it becomes a reference point. Future contributors can see what has already been attempted and build upon it, rather than unknowingly duplicating efforts.

 - **Improvement and Review:** Keeping the PR open allows for continuous review and suggestions for improvement. Other developers can provide feedback that might eventually lead to a viable implementation.

In summary, marking such PRs as drafts rather than closing them fosters collaboration, preserves valuable ideas, and helps maintain the continuity and history of the project.

body:
Just as an additional explanation for my view points in above comments (worded by gpt4o):

_When explaining why changing the code from using `if` to using `or` might introduce issues, it's important to highlight the differences in how these constructs handle falsy values. Here’s a detailed explanation:_

### Original Code:
```python
llm_temperature = (
    llm_temperature if llm_temperature is not None else llm_config.temperature
)
```

### Modified Code:
```python
llm_temperature = llm_temperature or llm_config.temperature
```

### Key Points to Explain:

1. **Handling of Falsy Values**:
   - **Original Code**: The expression `llm_temperature if llm_temperature is not None else llm_config.temperature` specifically checks if `llm_temperature` is `None`. If it's `None`, it uses `llm_config.temperature`; otherwise, it uses the value of `llm_temperature`. This means it only substitutes the default value if `llm_temperature` is explicitly `None`.
   - **Modified Code**: The expression `llm_temperature or llm_config.temperature` checks if `llm_temperature` is falsy (i.e., evaluates to `False` in a boolean context). In Python, values like `0`, `False`, `''` (empty string), and `[]` (empty list) are all considered falsy. Therefore, if `llm_temperature` is any of these values, `llm_config.temperature` will be used instead.

2. **Practical Implications**:
   - If `llm_temperature` is intended to accept values that could be falsy but still valid (e.g., `0` or `0.0` as a valid temperature), using `or` would incorrectly substitute these values with `llm_config.temperature`. This could lead to unexpected behavior and bugs.
   - The original code ensures that only a `None` value triggers the fallback to the configuration value, preserving the intended meaning of valid falsy values.

### Example Scenario:
Suppose `llm_temperature` can be `0.0`, which is a valid and meaningful value, but also falsy in a boolean context.

- **Original Code**: 
  ```python
  llm_temperature = 0.0  # Would remain 0.0
  ```
- **Modified Code**: 
  ```python
  llm_temperature = 0.0 or llm_config.temperature  # Would become llm_config.temperature, which is incorrect
  ```

### Conclusion:
By changing the code to use the `or` operator, you risk incorrectly handling valid falsy values. The original code's explicit check for `None` ensures that only an unset (`None`) value for `llm_temperature` triggers the fallback, preserving all other valid values, including falsy ones. This distinction is crucial for maintaining the correct and expected behavior of your function.

body:
> @enyst Are the remaining params necessary?

Some are used in evals. It's true it's not the same, at least since we introduced llm_config customization: they're now used by defining [multiple custom llm_configs](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/blob/main/evaluation/humanevalfix/README.md). Before that, one had to find other ways to override.

More to the point here, though: this PR is not proposing to remove them, but to change them when they have meaningful user-set values. And that seems that it would break not only common practice or our old use cases, but also OpenAI compatibility.

These parameters are the parameters defined by OpenAI API for the completion call. Think of all the ways that matters today. Open LLMs have a compatible API at least in part; applications like LMStudio offer a compatible API afaik; same for other proxies. LiteLLM has an explicit documented goal to keep OpenAI compatibility for other LLMs as much as possible. Research papers test on similar API, etc. Thousands (or more?) of lines of code out there use it.

Currently, someone who wants to adapt their agent to work with opendevin doesn't need to change their LLM code at all or almost: set it up to use our class and it just works. We haven't documented much, if at all, this drop-in compatibility feature, but it's real. [1] 

More importantly, they shouldn't need to debug forever why `temperature=0` that they send to our LLM doesn't behave the same way it did when they sent it to OpenAI API. Or directly to our own completion method, even.

(that said, I still think "model" is harmless 🤷. Happy to be proven otherwise.)

Side note:
As an example of how it matters, this CodeAct line: https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/blob/90ec0095dfe72e30114e093f2dc27c6bc75e8140/agenthub/codeact_agent/codeact_agent.py#L226
We don't have a `stop` variable. I didn't even have a clue there was such thing. But OpenAI does have a [`stop` parameter](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat/create#chat-create-stop), and CodeAct completion() call just works.
Please note that it also sets temperature=0.0.


[1] I think we should keep the signature as clearly as possible as "drop-in replacement" and that's why I'm nitpicking even the use of a different name ( "do_completion") for the completion function, though it's not a big deal, but it's [fixed here](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/commit/c234d82387349dbb1352e4ae22cc2cda0f211479).

body:
You already know my opinion on this issue. 😁 

Of course we _know_, that during regular _runtime_ the `workspace_mount_path` won't be `None`, even though it technically is optional _by use_ anyways.

But to just _shut up_ `mypy` for a single case, it is not a good enough reason. For that use a directive (`# type:ignore`) or a cleaner, common preceeding check like `if config.workspace_mount_path:`, as is common practice. This PR introduces more code changes than it would require to remedy the actual issue.

From an architectural view, `AppConfig` can be used standalone, obviously, without even calling any of its methods.
Right now, only the unit tests make direct use of the class, but that doesn't preclude other code from using it in the future.

From the outside, with this PR applied, it is totally intransparent, why suddenly an `UNDEFINED` value lands in that string.
No code then using the class, withouth calling all its methods, would have the expectation of this value occuring (not to mention, it isn't documented neither, yet).
Instead, this would force it to be coded to check for an extra enum value, that is otherwise not used or enforced anywhere else.

There are plenty of other occurences of `: str | None = None` for defaults. But I hope these won't get defaulted differently, neither, just because mypy _might_ object just in case something's not cleanly coded.

I'm really done discussing this either way, it's not up to me anyways. 🤣

I re-writte the comments a bit: https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/2460#issue-2355737537

Regarding ``The `agentskill` function currently returns nothing, which makes it hard for GPTSwarm to get a return value. This significantly influences the performance``:

I think the mechanism of OD is to output information in the terminal, and then CodeActAgent gets such information as an observation from the terminal. Right? Currently, I do not follow this and just want to directly get a return value from a function. However, I think OD GPTSwarm could also follow the CodeActAgent observation style.

Regarding ``For example, what file readers are needed?``:

In the original GPTSwarm [readers](https://github.com/metauto-ai/GPTSwarm/blob/main/swarm/environment/tools/reader/readers.py), many different readers are used, but in https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/1914 and the following https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/2016, some of them have been deleted. This likely influences more than the potentially solvable 2-5 questions, making them unsolvable in GAIA.

Regarding ``GPTSwarm is stateless (me)`` and ``I find you didn't implement the `step` function``:

Current OD GPTSwarm is followed some predefined human SOP or workflow in a graph-based design. I think OD GPTSwarm could fully follow the agenthub style (it may not be hard), but I am personally not 100% familiar with this, so I think help is needed here.

Regarding ``if currently agent skill and web navigation are not well done``:

I think the current web navigation is good but specific to some benchmarks. For GAIA or many applications, just returning compressed but informative observations is enough.

body:
I think this is a bigger discussion of three options:
1. Sub-agents
2. Tools
3. Documentation lookup ([DocPrompting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05987)/RAG)

I think all of these are reasonable options here, and each have their tradeoffs. Overall I'm pretty bullish on the third option, which would use a single agent and not create separate tools, but instead look up documentation about how to do things with code. This is more like how human programmers work, and seems to be a pretty nice and scalable option. (if you want, you could thumbs-up this message for "3")
author: neubig

body:
Yeah, I think "Documentation lookup ([DocPrompting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05987)/RAG)" pretty much aligns with what I'm thinking about for the next step of `agentskills` -- given task instruction, we can retrieve relevant tools for the agent; on the other hand, the agent can also proactively browse the `agentskills` library for more details (e.g., like a human developer browsing the doc site).

Right now, I'm a bit worried about bloating the `agentskills` library too much -- But i think it is acceptable now. Maybe after this PR, we should really start working on the tool retrieval functionality of `agentskills` library described in https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/1941 so that the system prompt can be a little bit more concise for the agent.

Just speaking to the agentskills and the generated system prompt, which was around 11 KB last time I checked (don't have the tokenized number).
Instead of pulling in the whole agentskills  docprompt collection, could we instead provide a strong hint like
"`For preferred file operations please ask for <insert keyword>.`"
so the LLM could ask OpenDevin for more details when needed, and then we send the full skills docs.
Obviously, there'd be mixed results, whether the LLM would even _care to ask_ and/or ignore this, but this just as a tangent idea.

As to this PR itself: the aim was to reduce roundtrips and token usage. Using the browser instead of the existing API is rather expensive, e.g. OpenDevin's repo page alone is over 400KB. And that might be multiplied by any number of times till the HTML parsing and clicking around by the LLM actually manages to extract the right information.

For the architectural location of it: since Github is a major topic for the project, could a specialized GithubAgent be an option?

body:
Updated workflow with the help of Sonnet 3.5 😀 :

1. It installs the required dependencies (toml and semver) for version comparison.
2. It fetches both the latest tag and the current pyproject.toml version.
3. It compares the versions using the semver library to determine the appropriate action:
If pyproject version > latest tag: create a new tag
If pyproject version < latest tag: update pyproject.toml
If versions are equal: do nothing
4. Based on the comparison result, it either updates the pyproject.toml file or creates a new tag.
This workflow will now handle both scenarios: updating pyproject.toml when a higher tag exists, and creating a new tag when the pyproject.toml version is higher than the current tag.

body:
@tobitege 
I understand the release process now. 😁 Tags are created manually, Then the release person can create the release from the tag. 
Maybe my script can give some help, it can update the version and create the tag. 
```shell
#!/bin/bash

# You can input "patch", "minor", "major", or a specific version like "0.6.3".
poetry version $1

# Get new version number
NEW_VERSION=$(poetry version -s)

# commit and create tag
git add pyproject.toml
git commit -m "Bump version to $NEW_VERSION"
git tag "$NEW_VERSION" 
```

Use it:
```shell
./bump_version.sh patch  # or minor/major/0.6.3
```

Then, the release person just needs to check it and, if everything is fine, submit it.
```shell
# then check and push it manually
git push --tags
```

author: enyst

body:
> I'm not sure exactly, it seems it can respond with different dict keys

You are right! It could be anything. Every micro-agent, for example, has its own schema defined in `agent.yaml`.

Why don't we simply make every agent return a natural language output in `content` field like `BrowsingAgent`? The reason is, some agents (especially micro-agents) are designed to do a very narrow task, and they may or may not want to answer in natural language. A SQL agent, for (imaginary) example, could return SQL execution results in any pre-defined format.

What we should do here is unclear to me. I don't know how we could design delegation better and more elegant.

With "--cached":
```sh
tobias@CD137K:/mnt/d/github$ git diff --cached
error: unknown option `cached'

Without:

tobias@CD137K:/mnt/d/github$ git diff
warning: Not a git repository. Use --no-index to compare two paths outside a working tree

author: iFurySt

body:
@li-boxuan I think we can't merge this, it doesn't work with delegates errors.

First, the issue we talked about is on `main` too, and there's a bit more, the behavior I see is like:
- it doesn't seem to reset the task/state, so the accumulated cost continues to apply. On `main`, one more action over budget goes through every step, it just happens starting from the next step, not the one with the error
- it blocks the ability of the user to ask for some other task, until they refresh or press stop (wiping history); even though the sandbox was restarted after the error, so the controller was re-initialized. (the reason for the latter might be that it's saved in state, and the state is restored implicitly if it can)

On `main`, with 0.1 budget per task:

![Image 2024-06-26 at 23 34](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/assets/6080905/994f91e0-38f2-4840-a866-a116c0a2fda3)

```
23:31:42 - opendevin:INFO: llm.py:239 - Cost: 0.02 USD | Accumulated Cost: 0.13 USD
23:31:42 - ACTION
**IPythonRunCellAction**
THOUGHT: I will first print the number 7, and then I will find out the current Vice President of the USA.
CODE:
print(7)
23:31:42 - OBSERVATION
ErrorObservation(content='Task budget exceeded. Current cost: 0.13, Max budget: 0.10', observation='error')
23:31:42 - opendevin:INFO: agent_controller.py:196 - [Agent Controller 65d1bfe0-16c7-4690-a534-5f8928d2163b] Setting agent(CodeActAgent) state from AgentState.RUNNING to AgentState.ERROR
```

But on the PR branch the delegates errors just don't work at all:
- when it gets the error, it gets "frozen". I want to say what happens has to do with the timing of the async. I think it leads to some deadlock where [this](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/blob/6099f72ae31a13b66b2deb625c7a0c3aa0fb3ff3/opendevin/controller/agent_controller.py#L266) error code got executed, the delegate got closed, but the parent still keeps a reference to it (not sure why we don't set it to None), so the parent still forwards to it [here](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/blob/6099f72ae31a13b66b2deb625c7a0c3aa0fb3ff3/opendevin/controller/agent_controller.py#L260). The delegate is in STOPPED state (iirc) [here](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/blob/6099f72ae31a13b66b2deb625c7a0c3aa0fb3ff3/opendevin/controller/agent_controller.py#L248), in which case this just goes back looping. So the two controllers just invite each other to step up and no one dares. 😅 
- it's not clear to me what exactly is missing there. Maybe we could consider ERROR state a sub-case of `delegate_done` along with FINISHED and REJECTED and try to finish it off in that block? After all, the delegate really won't continue, I suppose.

Either way, I think we can't merge this, because it breaks delegates errors worse than minor issues on main. FWIW I played a bit with it at the end of the step, and at the start of the step, same freeze. Gonna have to try to see if I broke it too when I merged... 😅

body:
> Thanks so much @amanape for the great feedback! I'll revise the execption handling further per your suggestions. With regard to detecting file changes from "outside" in order to notify the LLM: that's another can of worms, tbh. 🤣 At some point the user has to take some responsibility when editing files during a task run, either way.

@tobitege This is an important point, but I respectfully have a different viewpoint. While user responsibility is crucial, I believe we should implement a mechanism to track modifications made during a task run. For instance, we could add these changes to the history so that the LLM is aware of any edits the user makes. This way, we ensure that the LLM has the most up-to-date context, preventing potential issues like creating duplicate files, calling renamed functions incorrectly, or updating outdated line ranges like @amanape mentioned.

body:
Admittedly, my statement was a bit too flippant and I basically agree with you, that if there's a practical way to make this work without being too overcomplicated, we should look into this as a feature.

A while back I took a look at one potential rough way to do this, but discarded it since it might require an extra service.
Something along the line of this to assist in the agent skills:
```py
class FileChangeHandler(FileSystemEventHandler):
    def __init__(self):
        self.modified_files = set()

    def on_modified(self, event):
        if event.is_directory:
            return
        self.modified_files.add(event.src_path)

    def clear_modified_files(self):
        self.modified_files.clear()

file_change_handler = FileChangeHandler()
observer = Observer()
observer.schedule(file_change_handler, path='.', recursive=True)
observer.start()

def has_file_changed(file_path):
    changed = file_path in file_change_handler.modified_files
    file_change_handler.clear_modified_files()
    return changed
```

author: SmartManoj

body:
I don't oppose upgrading the default sandbox image's Python interpreter. But this should be unrelated to solving this issue, or you could say it's not necessary. I have a few questions:

1. How do you determine that most users use Python 3.11?
2. Users have diverse needs. Some need Python 3.11, some need 3.12, and some need Python 3.8. You said specifying custom_container_image is not ideal. So, what do you plan to do instead? In comparison, using a custom_container_image is a more versatile solution.

What I'm saying is, upgrading the default Python interpreter in the sandbox image isn't a bad thing, but users' custom needs should be addressed through custom sandbox images. You can't meet all users' needs with a general image.

> python3 will still point to v3.10

I think if we really need to upgrade to python 3.11, i'd root for pointing `python3` to `3.11` as well - so that we only have ONE version of Python in the sandbox as far as user knows?


Since now we already support custom images, instead of ONE default sandbox image, I wonder if we can start a mechanism to build *multiple* supported sandbox images from a list of images. e.g., `nodejs`, `python` with different version, etc. And we might also need to add a setting panel on the front end for users to choose the official image that they want to use.

I think this will likely be a more fundamental solution than simply upgrading our default sandbox image to python 3.11, because every user can just pick whatever container with whatever dependency that suits their needs?
